newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Jan 3.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Jan 3.

text.p: A senior policeman is at the centre of an investigation into "irregularities" after he was stopped at a drink-drive checkpoint before Christmas, Hutt acting district commander Paul Nickalls said on Thursday. Inspector Nickalls said an investigation into the incident had been completed and had been passed on to the region four commander, Assistant Commissioner Neville Trendle. Page 1.

The "stunning" news that the Australian government gave New Zealand A$20 million in return for defence commitments showed that all foreign policy commitments by New Zealand should be ratified by parliament, Alliance spokesman Matt Robson said on Thursday. It was staggering to find out from Australian documents that New Zealand had needed Australia to bail out of a balance-of-payments crisis in 1966, he said. Page 2.

Mental health services for children and young people come nowhere near meeting targets, the Health Ministry says. Services for children and young people under 20 are reaching less than 0.83 percent, compared with a five percent target set in government policy. "Adequacy of children and young people's mental health services is a particular concern given the high rates of youth suicide in New Zealand," the ministry said in post-election briefing papers. Page 2.

A decision on the future of fishing boat Maria Luisa, of which five members of the same family died in a collision with a container ship near the entrance to Wellington harbour on Sunday night, would be made on Friday, deputy habour-master John Dickison said on Thursday. Page 3.

Analysts say strong economic fundamentals point to another good year for New Zealand stocks in 1997 but they will be keeping a close eye on Wall Street. "If we do have a bad year it will be driven by overseas markets," said Jason Wong, a First NZ Capital economist. Page 12.

Telecom New Zealand shareholder Ameritech might on Friday become the first Baby Bell to seek United States Federal Communications Commission approval for long-distance phone services under a new law. The company, which provides local phone services in five mid-western states, will file with the commission for permission to provide long-distance phone servies in Michigan, a person close to the company said. Page 12.

Global securities firm Morgan Stanley & Co says it has suffered a "severe" loss at the hands of professional traders and wants the Securities and Exchange Commission to change United States trading rules. Page 12.

Hollinger chief executive Conrad Black has accused Australian politicians of juvenile behaviour and being impenetrably insular. Blue Star Group's appetite for office supplies and automation businesses appeared insatiable in 1996, and eventually drew the attention of the monopolies watchdog, the Commerce Commission. But this year expect more of the same from the company which, two years ago, had limited high-street visibility but now has to be careful not to overly increase its market dominance. "We will continue to grow in New Zealand, but we see more significant opportunities in Australia," chief executive Eric Watson said. Page 13.

Foster's Brewing subsidiary Carlton and United Breweries said on Thursday it had extended its takeover offer for Ballarat Brewing to February 7. Foster's launched the bid of A$2.50 (NZ$2.84) per Ballarat share on November 20. Page 13.
